A prolonged conflict will put pressure on India's twin deficits and drive rupee weaker. Impact on WPI inflation and hence corporate profit margin will be sharper than the retail inflation which could have an initial layer of shock absorber from the OMCs and then possibly via fuel tax cut. EQUITY The defining feature of Indian equity markets in 2026 so far, has been a significant surge in volatility. While January saw aggressive FPI selling amidst a weakening rupee, February began with an STT (Securities and Transactions Tax) hike on derivatives in the Union Budget. Trade deal announcements with the EU and more importantly the US, provided some cheer for the markets before fears of a potential disruption for Indian software services exports from AI (artificial intelligence) soured sentiment again.

The two-way volatility, however, resulted in broadly flat markets for February with the Nifty and the Sensex shedding 0.6% and 1.2% respectively for the month. with the US and corresponding easing of US tariffs on Indian exports. Other positives for Indian equities included a significant easing of premium versus other emerging markets owing to the sharp underperformance of the past six quarters and more importantly a likely improvement in corporate earnings. Revisions in earnings had stabilised after seeing downward revisions for a good part of CY25, signalling potential bottoming out. Trade deals could lift medium term earnings by improving visibility and reviving corporate expansion plans. Budget measures such as higher infra and manufacturing spends and incentivization of private capex on strategic sectors, past year's income tax and GST cuts, and the lagged impact of monetary easing, were also supportive of earnings going ahead. A reflation in economy and recovery in corporate earnings looked to be the base case.

However, entering March, the energy shock from the US- Israel- Iran conflict, has brought in a fresh bout of sell-off for Indian equities. This has led to a surge in crude oil and gas prices along with other commodities that act as substitutes such as coal or those that rely on energy for their own production such as aluminium. A prolonged disruption of Persian Gulf oil and gas exports could mean return to 2022-style energy prices which would have clear macro and market implications. In this scenario, inflation rises worldwide, more so in Europe and Asia. Central banks may initially look through the shock, but persistently higher energy prices risk unanchoring inflation expectations. Growth slows as household real incomes are squeezed and corporate margins weaken from higher input costs. Current accounts deteriorate across energy-importing economies such as India, pressuring currencies. In such an environment, global capital could also rotate away from equities further aggravating the macro crises.

While it is difficult to know how long the current shutdown lasts and consequently to what extent the energy crises persist, the base case is for the situation to be resolved sooner rather than later given the disastrous economic consequences for almost everyone involved. In this scenario, reflation of the economy and earnings recovery return into play. That said, a longer disruption, as outlined above, cannot entirely be ruled out as a risk scenario. On asset allocation, we continue to be neutral equities expecting positive albeit moderate returns, with preference for large caps over mid and small caps on relative valuations. Relative valuations favour large caps

FIXED INCOME Enabling policy rate transmission and ensuring smoother absorption of market borrowing has been the objective of RBI market operations since the last policy review. Towards this, the central bank has ensured that the operating target and more importantly collateralized overnight rates stay materially lower than the policy rate. This has enabled market yields to stay anchored with a modest retracement over the previous month. However, the levels have moved back over the last few days with the escalating middle east crisis. Source: Bloomberg, SBIFM Research Source: SBIFM Research Liquidity Operations & Money Market Segment The most obvious shift in terms of RBI actions has been the tolerance for higher banking liquidity and weighted average call rates staying within the corridor rather than being aligned closer to the repo rate.

corridor rather than being aligned closer to the repo rate. Effectively this has translated into collateralized rates that are the main anchor for pricing in all money market segments trading below the SDF. Recent weeks have seen the RBI resume screen-based OMO purchases to counterbalance the likely forex market intervention. The immediate impact of surplus liquidity has been with respect to money market rates that have been largely capped at around 7% in the 3 month and 1-year segments. Even as further upticks have been capped, the large supply pressure so far as well as anticipated supply in the pipeline would keep rates elevated in the near future. Reversal of this seasonality is expected around the end of the quarter and moving into the coming quarter. Higher supply keeps CD spreads elevated. The recent geopolitical developments add an additional layer of risk on the overall macro environment with possible upside inflation pressures if crude prices were to stay elevated. This would also impact RBI's reaction function in various market segments. In the near term, the significant presence of RBI across the forex and rates markets have clearly anchored market yields. However, the risk of external negative factors sustaining/ worsening should also be assessed.

Hence, apart from tactical positioning largely based on the seasonality factors around fiscal year end, we would continue to remain anchored to maintaining duration positioning at a moderate level. Overall, on a risk–reward basis, spreads on high grade bonds as well as selective credits at the shorter-end remain attractive. Strategies on duration would continue to be nimble, with preference to remain relatively lighter on a directional basis. Curve steepness is expected to remain intact in the coming months. Short tenor high grade bond funds continue to provide higher accrual, wider spreads as well as an optimum risk/reward that provide opportunities over the coming months as well as into the coming year.
